angle: angle 1 · a place and a time
title: Debunking the Biggest Myths About 1950s America

scenes.text: Ask anyone what the nineteen fifties were like, and you'll hear the same picture. A white picket fence. A mother in pearls, vacuuming in high heels. A father in a suit, home at five-thirty. Two perfect children, a dog, and a new car in the driveway. Everyone was happy, everyone was rich, and nothing ever went wrong.
scenes.caption: THE PICTURE WE ALL KNOW

scenes.text: Some of that picture is true. A lot of it isn't. Much of what we think we know about the fifties comes from television shows and advertisements that were made to sell a dream. The real decade was more interesting, more complicated, and in some ways, much more surprising.
scenes.caption: MORE COMPLICATED

scenes.text: So today, let's take the biggest myths about nineteen fifties America, one by one, and hold each of them up to the facts. Some of them will surprise you. A few of them might even change how you remember your own childhood.
scenes.caption: MYTH VS FACT

scenes.text: But first, a quick thought. If you lived through the fifties, you already know some of this. You remember things the history books leave out. So as we go, ask yourself whether each myth matches what you saw with your own eyes, in your own town, at your own kitchen table.
scenes.caption: WHAT DID YOU SEE?

scenes.text: The first myth is that everyone in the fifties lived in a new house in the suburbs. It's true that the suburbs exploded. Places like Levittown went up almost overnight, and millions of young families moved out of the cities. It was one of the biggest migrations in American history.
scenes.caption: THE SUBURBS EXPLODED
scenes.chapter: Myth 1: Everyone lived in the suburbs

scenes.text: The first Levittown houses sold for under eight thousand dollars, and with the G.I. Bill, a returning veteran could often move in with almost nothing down. For a young couple who had grown up in the Depression, a small house with a yard of their own felt like a miracle. That part of the dream was very real.
scenes.caption: UNDER $8,000

scenes.text: But in nineteen sixty, after a whole decade of suburban growth, only about one in three Americans lived in the suburbs. The rest lived in big cities, small towns and on farms. Millions still lived in old apartment buildings in crowded city neighborhoods, or in farmhouses without indoor plumbing.
scenes.caption: ONLY ONE IN THREE

scenes.text: In fact, in nineteen fifty, about a third of American homes still had no complete indoor plumbing at all. No bathtub or shower, or no flush toilet, or no hot water. In the rural South and in parts of the countryside, the outhouse in the backyard was still a fact of daily life well into the fifties.
scenes.caption: NO INDOOR PLUMBING

scenes.text: The second myth is that mothers in the fifties never worked outside the home. The television mothers didn't. June Cleaver never went to an office. But the real numbers tell a different story.
scenes.caption: JUNE CLEAVER DIDN'T WORK

scenes.text: In the nineteen fifties, about one in three American women worked for pay, and the number was rising every year. By nineteen sixty, around thirty percent of married women had jobs. They were secretaries, nurses, teachers, factory workers, telephone operators, waitresses and shop clerks.
scenes.caption: ONE IN THREE WOMEN WORKED

scenes.text: Many of those women had already proven themselves during the war. Millions had built ships, planes and tanks while the men were overseas. When the soldiers came home, a lot of them were let go to make room for the returning veterans. But many never forgot what they had done, and plenty of them went right back to work.
scenes.caption: THEY HAD DONE IT BEFORE

scenes.text: Many of them went back to work once their children were in school, to help pay for the house, the car or college. And for poor families, immigrant families and Black families, a mother's paycheck had never been optional. The stay-at-home mother was real, but she was never the whole story.
scenes.caption: NEVER THE WHOLE STORY

scenes.text: The third myth is that everyone in the fifties was comfortable, with a good job and money to spare. It was a boom decade. Wages rose. The middle class grew faster than at any time in American history. Families bought cars, televisions and washing machines at an astonishing rate.
scenes.caption: A BOOM DECADE

scenes.text: And a lot of that buying was done on credit. The Diners Club card appeared in nineteen fifty, and by the end of the decade, installment plans were everywhere. A family could take home a new refrigerator or a new Chevrolet for a few dollars down and a few dollars a month. Household debt grew quickly through the whole decade.
scenes.caption: A FEW DOLLARS DOWN

scenes.text: And yet, in the late fifties, more than one in five Americans lived below the poverty line, according to the government's own later figures. That was around forty million people. Poverty was especially deep in Appalachia, the rural South, Indian reservations and the inner cities.
scenes.caption: ONE IN FIVE WAS POOR

scenes.text: Most middle-class families in the new suburbs simply didn't see it. Michael Harrington's book, The Other America, published in nineteen sixty-two, shocked many readers who had no idea how many of their fellow citizens were going without enough to eat. For millions of Americans, the boom never arrived.
scenes.caption: THE OTHER AMERICA

scenes.text: The fourth myth is that life in the fifties was safer. In some ways, it felt that way. Children roamed free. Doors stayed unlocked. Crime rates in many places were lower than they would be in later decades.
scenes.caption: IT FELT SAFER

scenes.text: But in other ways, daily life was far more dangerous. Cars had no seat belts, no airbags and steel dashboards that could kill in a crash. In nineteen fifty-five, the death rate on American roads, per mile driven, was several times higher than it is today.
scenes.caption: NO SEAT BELTS

scenes.text: And then there were cigarettes. In the mid-fifties, close to half of all American adults smoked. Doctors appeared in cigarette advertisements. People smoked in offices, in restaurants, on airplanes, in hospitals and even in front of their children in the car with the windows rolled up. Almost nobody thought twice about it.
scenes.caption: HALF OF ADULTS SMOKED

scenes.text: Children rode bicycles without helmets and played with toys that would be banned today. And then there was polio. Every summer, parents lived in fear of it. In nineteen fifty-two alone, there were about fifty-eight thousand cases in the United States. Swimming pools and movie theaters closed when an outbreak hit town.
scenes.caption: THE SUMMER FEAR

scenes.text: When Jonas Salk's vaccine was declared safe and effective in April of nineteen fifty-five, church bells rang and people cried in the streets. Within a few years, polio cases dropped dramatically. It was one of the happiest days of the decade, precisely because the fear before it had been so real.
scenes.caption: APRIL 1955

scenes.text: The fifth myth is that fifties teenagers were polite, obedient kids who went to sock hops and drank milkshakes. Many of them did. But the grown-ups of the fifties were convinced that teenagers were out of control.
scenes.caption: THE SOCK HOP

scenes.text: In nineteen fifty-four, the United States Senate held hearings on juvenile delinquency. Comic books were blamed for corrupting children, and the comic book industry created a strict code to censor itself. Parents worried about hot rods, switchblades, leather jackets and, above all, rock and roll.
scenes.caption: THE SENATE WORRIED

scenes.text: When Elvis Presley appeared on television in nineteen fifty-six, some ministers called his music sinful, and one famous broadcast showed him only from the waist up. To many parents, rock and roll sounded like the end of civilization. Their children, of course, loved every note of it.
scenes.caption: FROM THE WAIST UP

scenes.text: And fifties teenagers grew up fast. In nineteen fifty-six, the typical American woman married for the first time at about twenty, and many brides were still in their teens. Plenty of young couples had their first baby before they turned twenty-one. Adulthood didn't wait for anyone in those years.
scenes.caption: MARRIED AT TWENTY

scenes.text: The sixth myth is that the fifties were a carefree time when nobody worried about anything. In reality, Americans lived under the shadow of the atomic bomb. The Soviet Union tested its first atomic bomb in nineteen forty-nine, and the fear of nuclear war hung over the entire decade.
scenes.caption: THE SHADOW OF THE BOMB

scenes.text: Schoolchildren practiced duck and cover drills, crouching under their desks with their hands over their heads. Some families built bomb shelters in their backyards or basements, stocked with canned food and water. Cities tested air raid sirens on a regular schedule, and every child knew the sound.
scenes.caption: DUCK AND COVER

scenes.text: Then, in October of nineteen fifty-seven, the Soviet Union launched Sputnik, the first satellite ever to orbit the Earth. Americans went outside at night to watch it pass overhead. Suddenly the country worried that it was falling behind, and within a year, Congress passed a law pouring money into science and math in American schools.
scenes.caption: OCTOBER 1957: SPUTNIK

scenes.text: There was also fear of a different kind. During the Red Scare, people lost their jobs because of rumors that they had communist sympathies. Teachers, actors, writers and government workers were investigated. Many Americans learned to be careful about what they said, and to whom.
scenes.caption: THE RED SCARE

scenes.text: And the biggest myth of all is that the fifties were the same for everyone. For many white middle-class families, it was a golden age. But for Black Americans, especially in the South, segregation was the law. Separate schools, separate water fountains, separate seats on the bus.
scenes.caption: NOT THE SAME FOR EVERYONE
scenes.chapter: Myth 7: It was the same for everyone

scenes.text: The fifties were also when that began to change. In nineteen fifty-four, the Supreme Court ruled in Brown versus Board of Education that segregated schools were unconstitutional. In nineteen fifty-five, Rosa Parks refused to give up her seat on a bus in Montgomery, Alabama, and the bus boycott that followed lasted more than a year.
scenes.caption: 1955: MONTGOMERY

scenes.text: In nineteen fifty-seven, nine Black students walked into Central High School in Little Rock, Arkansas, protected by soldiers of the United States Army. The fifties weren't only an age of contentment. They were the beginning of one of the great moral struggles in American history.
scenes.query: Little Rock Nine 1957 Central High School
scenes.caption: 1957: LITTLE ROCK

scenes.text: Women faced limits too. In much of the country, a married woman could have trouble opening a credit account or getting a loan without her husband's signature. Many employers fired women as soon as they became pregnant. Those rules would only begin to change in the sixties and seventies.
scenes.caption: HER HUSBAND'S SIGNATURE

scenes.text: So, was everything we remember about the fifties a myth? No. A lot of it was real. The economy really did boom. Families really did buy houses on one paycheck. Neighbors really did know each other. Kids really did play outside until dark. Many people really were happier with less.
scenes.caption: A LOT OF IT WAS REAL

scenes.text: A gallon of gas cost around twenty-nine cents. A movie ticket was well under a dollar. A good state university could cost a few hundred dollars a year. And a man with a high school diploma could often find a factory job that paid enough to support a whole family. Those numbers are not a myth.
scenes.caption: 29 CENTS A GALLON

scenes.text: The truth is that the fifties were both. A decade of hope and fear, of plenty and poverty, of tight communities and deep divisions. Like every decade, it was more complicated than the picture on the postcard. And that makes it more interesting, not less.
scenes.caption: BOTH AT ONCE

scenes.text: If you grew up in the fifties, your memories are true. The ones of the porch, the station wagon and the corner drugstore. They're just one part of a bigger, more surprising story. And that story is still being told, by everyone who was there.
scenes.caption: YOUR MEMORIES ARE TRUE

scenes.text: So tell us in the comments. Which of these myths surprised you, and what do you think people today get wrong about the fifties? We read every comment. And stay with us, because next we're looking at what it was like to retire in nineteen seventy-five. Thank you for spending this time with me.
scenes.caption: WHAT DO PEOPLE GET WRONG?
